taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes Rittmeyer et al. (2021) suggested peninsular Florida populations be elevated to a separate species, O. carinatus.
fieldMarks: Small, thin snake, uniform green above; underside, chin and lip scales yellowish-green to cream.
Juveniles resemble smaller adults but are lighter in colour.
Females longer and heavier; males have a longer tail; average lengths about 947 mm (females) and 892 mm (males).
behavior: Diurnal and largely arboreal; sleeps coiled on branch ends near shorelines, less arboreal in spring and fall.
Insectivore hunting by sight: crickets, grasshoppers, caterpillars and spiders.
Flees into dense vegetation rather than biting; active roughly April-November in the north, hibernates in winter; may nest communally.
habitat: Dense vegetation (vines, shrubs, trees) near water, at forest edges and in fairly open forests, overgrown pasture, thickets and marsh edges.
range: Southeastern United States, north to southern New Jersey, through Florida to the Keys, west to central Oklahoma and Texas and into northern Mexico. Not in Canada.
